name: PT MNC Energy Investments Tbk

frontmatter.title: Karya Pacific Energy — a quota-bound coal ramp at a premium price
frontmatter.summary: IATA has a signed contractor ramp toward 7.0 Mt and 298 Mt of reserves, but its low-calorie coal realises a deep quality discount, cash opex takes more than a third of revenue and the balance sheet is tight. We exclude the APE fleet build from sustaining capex and price the product off HBA III; the DCF gives Rp76 and the market pays Rp94. REDUCE, target Rp72.
thesis: The volume ramp is real — a five-year KPP Mining contract and a 298 Mt reserve base support a move toward 7.0 Mt — but the cash economics are thin: even at US$25.9m of EBITDA, US$7.5m of capex, tax and working capital leave only US$9.4m of FCFF.

The product is low-calorie thermal coal priced off HBA III [S8], not the 6,000 kcal Newcastle benchmark: the war-premium Newcastle tape does not flow through to IATA's realised price, and the company's own HBA III estimate for 2026 is below the 2025 average [S8 p.86].

The sustaining capex is the direct-ownership portion of FY2025 fixed-asset additions — US$4.1m of US$12.6m — not the whole line: the right-of-use mining fleet (US$8.5m) is the APE start-up build and is growth, not maintenance [S12 Note 10].
Earnings do not convert into equity cash: FY2025 net profit was US$7.6m against operating cash flow of US$3.2m and capex of US$25.2m, leaving net debt at US$52.6m.

Liquidity is tight and the H1-2026 balance sheet is weaker: inventories of US$37.6m against cash of US$1.2m, factoring liabilities of US$8.1m, and current liabilities of US$69.7m above current assets of US$54.0m [S13]. A stockpile writedown and the Series B refinancing are live risks.

At Rp94 the market pays 20.4x forward EV/EBITDA for a capital-intensive, low-realisation producer; our blended value is Rp72, a -23.2% return. The control change to PT Karya Pacific Investama remains optionality, not a funded plan.

catalysts.event: Series B bond reached maturity; repayment or refinancing terms not yet disclosed
ESDM decision on the mid-year RKAB revision and the 2026 quota
Q3 2026 results and the H2 volume recovery
First full year of the KPP Mining contract ramp toward the long-run volume

blocks.text: **REDUCE, target Rp72, -23.2% expected return.** The company — formerly PT MNC Energy Investments Tbk and now PT Karya Pacific Energy Tbk — is a small South Sumatra thermal-coal producer with three operating IUP-OPs, a signed five-year mining-services contract with KPP Mining that points toward 7.0 Mt a year, and 298 Mt of stated reserves [S3, S11, S8]. The equity story the market is paying for is a successful RKAB-driven volume ramp under a new controlling shareholder. Our base case delivers that ramp — FY2027E volume of 6.5 Mt — and values the equity at Rp76 per share on the DCF. That is above the old target because the sustaining capex now excludes the APE fleet build, but still below the market price: the product realises a deep quality discount to HBA III, cash costs and shipping absorb most of the revenue, and the balance sheet has little room for error [S8, S12].

The variant view is not that the coal is not there. It is that IATA's cash conversion is worse than the P&L suggests, and the market is paying for a better price-and-capex mix than the company's own numbers support. In FY2025 the company earned US$7.6m of net profit but generated US$3.2m of operating cash flow and spent US$25.2m on fixed assets and mining properties, so net debt rose to US$52.6m [S12]. On the company's own volume plan the model reaches US$25.9m of EBITDA, but capex of US$7.5m, tax and working capital leave only US$9.4m of FCFF [S12, S8]. We have corrected the capex line so that the fleet build is treated as growth, not maintenance; even on that corrected basis the equity is a discounted residual, not a growth multiple.

What moves the value is narrow and identifiable. First, the low-calorie price: IATA sells 3,400 kcal/kg GAR coal, and the company's own HBA III estimate for 2026 is 32.0 USD/t to 35.0 USD/t [S8 p.86], below the 2025 HBA III average of 36.5 USD/t [S8]. Second, the RKAB quota: the 2026 national target was cut, only 2.0 Mt was approved as IATA's initial 2026 quota and its 7.8 Mt request was still being processed; the H1 revenue decline was explicitly attributed to the quota [S6, S8, S5]. Third, capex discipline and liquidity: the port and conveyor programme and the mining-property acquisitions are real cash calls, and the H1-2026 balance sheet carries inventories of US$37.6m, factoring liabilities of US$8.1m and cash of US$1.2m [S5, S12, S13].

The market is not pricing our base case, but the gap is narrower than the old SELL implied. At Rp94 the shares trade on 20.4x forward EV/EBITDA and 58.9x forward P/E, and the reverse DCF says the current price requires the FY2027E Newcastle benchmark to be 1.2 times our deck path, or about US$137/t, with IATA's quality discount unchanged [S0, S8]. Translated at our long-run realisation, that is an ASP close to the HBA III marker, not a repeat of the high-calorie war premium. That is a modest premium to the deck, not an absurd one — which is why the rating is REDUCE rather than SELL. We would revisit the rating on a sourced, contracted volume path with lower capex intensity, a visible improvement in the realised-to-HBA spread, a refinancing that removes the liquidity overhang, or a corporate action that puts cash or assets into the listed entity.

IATA is a South Sumatra coal name whose history illustrates the difference between a mining licence and a mining business. The group assembled a large resource position around Musi Banyuasin, brought three concessions into production, and then had to fund the ramp through a mixture of debt, a rights issue and asset sales. The equity has always been a minority-float story: the controlling block changed hands, the free float is small, and the stock has spent time on the exchange's special monitoring board after a prolonged low price. None of that is unusual for an Indonesian small-cap coal producer, but it means the shares trade on flow and narrative as much as on discounted cash flow.

PT Karya Pacific Energy Tbk is an Indonesian coal-mining group listed on the IDX under the ticker IATA. It was founded in 1968 as PT Indonesia Transport & Infrastructure Tbk, an aviation-services business, and was renamed PT MNC Energy Investments Tbk in February 2022 when it pivoted to coal [S12 Note 1]. It now operates as PT Karya Pacific Energy Tbk, the name adopted after the change of controlling shareholder; the 22 June 2026 AGMS approved the FY2025 accounts and a new board, while the FY2025 annual report is still filed under the old name [S4, S6]. The group now manages six IUP-OP licences in Musi Banyuasin, South Sumatra, of which three are fully operating — PT Indonesia Batu Prima Energi (IBPE), PT Putra Muba Coal (PMC) and PT Arthaco Prima Energy (APE) [S8]. The remaining permits are at various stages of development or extension [S12 Note 1g].

The revenue base is coal, with a small port-management and services line. FY2025 revenue was US$79.6m, split roughly half domestic and half export, plus a port-management fee [S12 Note 29]. The domestic leg sells into the Indonesian power and industrial market; the export leg ships low-calorie thermal coal to buyers in Asia. The customer list is concentrated: a small number of counterparties account for more than a tenth of revenue each, including PT Satria Jaya Energi, SAAI Resources and Visa Resources [S12 Note 29; S13 Note 29]. That concentration is normal for a sub-scale producer but it weakens IATA's pricing leverage and adds counterparty risk.

The operating model is contractor-led. In December 2025 IATA signed a five-year mining-services contract with PT Kalimantan Prima Persada (KPP Mining), an Astra-group contractor, covering coal getting, hauling and related work, with output targeted to rise from a lower first-year rate toward the long-run rate [S11]. The company also owns and is expanding port and conveyor infrastructure; management flagged a port and conveyor programme to support the recovery [S5]. That model lowers the company's direct labour and equipment risk but converts a large share of the cost base into contractor fees and shipping, which is why the cash-cost line is the key swing factor in the model.

Footprint and market position are modest. IATA's FY2025 production of 3.4 Mt is a small fraction of Indonesia's 790 Mt national output [S8]. It is a challenger, not a leader: it has no pricing power, no brand, no switching costs for its customers, and no control over the RKAB quota that determines how much it can sell. Its advantages are the reserve base — 298 Mt of stated reserves and 1,438 Mt of resources — and the fact that the three operating mines and the port infrastructure are already in place [S8, S12]. Those are real assets; the question for the equity is what they earn, not whether they exist.

Ownership and control changed materially in 2025-26. At 31 December 2025 PT Karya Pacific Investama held 48.8% of the shares and MNC Asia Holding held 18.8%; by October 2026 Karya Pacific Investama held 60.4% and the company stated it was no longer part of the MNC/Hary Tanoesoedibjo group [S12 Note 27; S4]. The free float is only 7.2%, and the FY2025 accounts still name MNC Asia Holding as the ultimate parent and Hary Tanoesoedibjo as the ultimate beneficial owner, which is a reminder that the control transition was completed after the balance-sheet date [S12 Note 1; S4]. The new controller's strategic intentions are not disclosed in any archived source; we do not assume an asset injection.

A coal-mining group in South Sumatra typically operates through a set of concession-holding subsidiaries, with the listed parent providing the balance sheet and the permits sitting in the operating companies. The contractor model is common: a mining-services firm brings the fleet and the crews, and the concession holder pays a per-tonne or per-bcm rate. That structure can scale production quickly, but it also means the concession holder's margin is the spread between the coal price and the contractor, hauling and port costs, and it makes the cash-cost line the most important number in the investment case.

Indonesia is the world's third-largest coal producer. National output reached 790 Mt in 2025, above the RKAB target of 740 Mt, of which 254 Mt went to the domestic market and 514 Mt was exported [S8]. The government has set the 2026 RKAB target at 600 Mt, a cut, explicitly to support prices after the 2025 oversupply [S8]. That policy is the single most important industry variable for IATA: only 2.0 Mt was approved as the initial 2026 quota, the company's request for 7.8 Mt was still being processed in August, and management was pursuing a mid-year revision [S6, S8, S5]. A quota-constrained producer cannot grow faster than the regulator allows, whatever its contractor or reserve base says.

Prices are weak at the low-calorie end, which is where IATA sells. The HBA III reference for 3,400 kcal/kg GAR coal averaged US$36.5/t in 2025 and is estimated by the company at 32.0 USD/t to 35.0 USD/t for 2026; the ICI-5 index averaged US$35.2/t in 2025 and is projected in a similar range [S8]. The high-calorie HBA averaged US$111/t in 2025 and is expected lower in 2026, while the Newcastle 6,000 kcal benchmark in our coal deck is US$150/t spot and US$118/t for FY2027E, with a long-run anchor of US$105/t [S8, deck]. The spread between Newcastle and HBA III is the single best explanation of why IATA's realised price is so far below the headline thermal-coal price: it is not selling 6,000 kcal coal, and the war-premium bid for high-grade seaborne coal does not reach its product. The Newcastle series is therefore only a forecastable scaling index; the HBA III realisation is the economic anchor, and the company's own 2026 estimate is the basis for our FY2026E ASP [S8].

The regulatory framework has three moving parts. The RKAB quota sets annual production and sales allowances. The domestic market obligation requires a share of output to be sold domestically, and the government has considered raising the DMO share above a quarter of production [S8]. The DHE SDA export-proceeds rule sets how much foreign-currency revenue must be retained or converted, and the government has revised the conversion limit [S8]. For IATA, the practical effect is that a larger share of revenue may be rupiah-denominated and subject to domestic price expectations, which caps the benefit of any export-price recovery. The company is an IUP-OP holder, so its royalty follows the IUP schedule rather than the IUPK schedule; the LK shows an effective royalty of 7.1% of revenue in FY2025, which is the rate we model [S12 Note 30].

Competitive positioning is weak on the five-forces test. Rivalry is high: Indonesia has hundreds of coal producers and the marginal tonne is price-taking. Buyer power is high: a handful of customers account for more than a tenth of revenue each [S12 Note 29]. Supplier power is moderate: the KPP Mining contract is a large, concentrated relationship, but it is a services contract and the contractor is replaceable in principle. Threat of entry is low for new mines because of permitting and capital, but the threat of substitution is high in the long run as renewable capacity and LNG displace thermal coal; the IEA expects global coal demand to fall from 8.8 bn t in 2025 to 8.6 bn t by 2030 [S8]. IATA has no moat beyond its licences, reserves and infrastructure, and those protect its ability to produce, not its ability to earn a return on capital.

The market-share picture is simple: IATA is a sub-one-per-cent producer in a 790 Mt national market, and its share will rise or fall with the RKAB, not with competitive wins [S8]. The company's addressable growth is therefore policy-driven. That is why the report treats the RKAB revision as a catalyst and the quota as a risk, rather than treating volume as a management execution variable.

Thermal-coal markets are cyclical and policy-sensitive, and the low-calorie end is the least defensible part of the curve. Low-rank coal is abundant, cheap to mine in Sumatra and Kalimantan, and burns at a lower efficiency, so it clears at a discount to high-grade seaborne benchmarks and is the first to be displaced when power generators can switch to gas or renewables. Indonesian producers have historically responded to price peaks by raising output, which is why the government uses RKAB quotas to manage supply. The result is a sector where the best operators earn returns through cost position and capital discipline, not through price.

IATA's reported history is a story of falling revenue and volatile margins. Revenue was US$192.1m in FY2022, US$170.1m in FY2023, US$117.9m in FY2024 and US$79.6m in FY2025 [S0]. The decline was driven by lower coal prices and a change in product quality, not by a collapse in volume: FY2024 sales were 3.7 Mt and FY2025 sales were 3.5 Mt, while FY2024 production was 4.1 Mt and FY2025 production was 3.4 Mt [S10, S8]. FY2025 revenue fell because the realised price fell faster than volume: the domestic ASP dropped and the export ASP fell to US$22.2/t [S8]. The first half of 2026 continued the pattern, with revenue of US$33.4m and net profit attributable to parent of US$1.0m [S13]. Our FY2026E revenue of US$68.0m is the H1 actual plus a partial H2 recovery at 3.2 Mt, with an implied ASP of 20.8 USD/t that sits inside the company's HBA III 2026 range rather than at the Newcastle war-premium price [S8 p.86, S13].

The cost structure is the heart of the investment case. FY2025 direct costs were US$35.1m, of which royalties were US$5.7m and the depreciation charged in direct costs was US$2.1m; the remaining cash cost was about US$7.8 per tonne [S12 Note 30]. Selling expenses were US$28.9m in total including operating expenses, dominated by coal shipping [S12 Notes 31/32]. That is a high cost stack for a product realising only a fraction of the HBA III marker: the model's cash margin per tonne is thin, and a small move in freight, fuel or the contractor rate moves EBITDA materially. The FY2024 cost base was even worse — subcontractor costs of US$12.2m and a different mine mix pushed the cash cost far above the FY2025 rate — which is why the FY2025 improvement is real but not yet proven through a full cycle [S12 Note 30]. The FY2025 effective tax rate was 15.0% [S12 P&L]; no concession is disclosed, so we hold that rate for the explicit forecast and step to the statutory 22.0% thereafter [S12 Note 2n].

D&A is the line where the Yahoo data pack is wrong and the LK matters. The pack's D&A line is a small fraction of the audited charge, which would imply an implausibly long asset life on a PP&E base of US$143.7m; the audited LK shows total fixed-asset depreciation of US$2.4m in FY2025 and US$2.2m in FY2024, with no mine-property amortisation charged to production in FY2025 [S12 Note 10/11]. We restate the history from the LK and carry D&A of US$0.7 per tonne in the forecast. The restatement raises EBITDA relative to a naive pack-based model, but it is the correct accounting: the depreciation is real, even though it is non-cash.

The cash-flow statement is less flattering than the P&L. FY2025 operating cash flow was US$3.2m, against net profit of US$8.3m, because working capital and tax absorbed the difference [S12 cash-flow statement]. Capex was US$25.2m, including mining-property acquisitions, so free cash flow was negative US$-27.4m [S12]. The fixed-asset part of that capex was US$12.6m [S12 Note 10]; it splits into US$4.1m of direct-ownership additions and US$8.5m of right-of-use mining equipment, the APE start-up fleet. We treat the fleet as growth, not sustaining maintenance, and carry 1.16 per tonne of sustaining capex, the direct-ownership portion over FY2025 sales [F2, F43] [S12]. The company funded the gap with a rights issue and new bank borrowing; net debt ended the year at US$52.6m [S12]. That is the core of our caution: the business is not yet generating the cash needed to fund its own growth, and the equity has been the residual financier.

The balance sheet is tighter at the H1-2026 date. Cash was US$1.2m, inventories US$37.6m, factoring liabilities US$8.1m, current liabilities US$69.7m against current assets US$54.0m [S13]. The coal inventory alone is US$26.6m [S13 Note 8], and H1 direct costs were US$21.3m [S13], so the stockpile covers more than a year of cost of sales; a quality or unsold-tonne problem would force an NRV writedown. At 31 December 2025 cash was US$2.2m against total debt of US$54.7m; the debt includes rupiah bonds whose Series B tranche reached its 6 October 2026 maturity, plus bank facilities from Mayapada and Victoria [S12 Notes 18/19/20]. The archive records neither repayment nor refinancing of the matured tranche [S12]. The company has no committed undrawn facility disclosed in the archive, which is why we treat refinancing as a risk rather than a base-case assumption. We hold gross debt flat in the forecast (no net new borrowing and no repayment), which implicitly assumes the tranche is refinanced at maturity; the modelled cost of debt is the blended rate, and refinancing at a higher coupon would lower the equity value.

Capital allocation has been growth-first. The company has never paid a dividend, and the FY2025 accounts record no distribution [S0, S12]. Cash has gone into mining-property acquisitions, the APE start-up and the port/conveyor programme. Our forecast carries a zero payout — not because we think the company should never pay one, but because there is no record or policy that supports a dividend, and the capex programme has first call on cash [S12, S5]. The dividend-capacity anchor therefore does not apply to the paid stream; the valuation section discusses capacity rather than a current yield.

Earnings-quality flags, run through the house screen. The accruals ratio is modest: FY2025 net profit of US$8.3m against operating cash flow of US$3.2m on total assets of US$238.3m is a low single-digit percentage, so there is no evidence of earnings outrunning cash in the accounting sense [S12]. The bigger issue is the opposite: cash conversion is weak because capex and working capital are heavy, not because revenue is fictitious. Receivables fell with revenue. Inventory is the flag: US$37.6m at H1-2026, of which coal is US$26.6m [S13 Note 8], against H1 direct costs of US$21.3m [S13]; that is more than a year of cost of sales and is not a normal working stock, so an NRV writedown or an unsold-tonne/quality problem is a live risk. Related-party liabilities were about six per cent of total liabilities at FY2025, mostly trade payables to PT Karya Pacific Shipping and other MNC entities, which is disclosed but worth monitoring as the control group changes [S12 Note 26]. The H1-2026 cash-flow statement also shows new related-party other-payables funding as cash fell [S13].

Two IDX regime flags need to be stated plainly. The shares entered the special monitoring board in 2024 after the average price fell below the exchange's threshold, which imposed full call auction on the stock [S15]. The September 2026 list of stocks removed from the special board does not include IATA, so the current status is unresolved in the archive and must be checked with the exchange before any position is sized [S14]. The free float is only 7.2%, which magnifies the liquidity and governance risk [S0]. Neither point is a manipulation finding; both are investability constraints that belong in the risk section, not in a valuation premium.

The reported profit of a coal miner and its cash generation can diverge sharply because the P&L carries depreciation, depletion and reclamation accruals that are non-cash, while the cash-flow statement carries the capex that replaces the depleted asset. A producer can look profitable for years while consuming equity if it keeps buying mining properties and equipment. That is why a coal analysis starts with the cash-cost per tonne and the capex intensity, then tests the P&L against the cash-flow statement, rather than taking the net margin at face value.

We value IATA on a life-of-asset DCF at through-cycle prices, cross-checked against EV/EBITDA at the peer median, a dividend-capacity yield and EV/reserves. That method set fits a coal producer because the asset is finite, the price is cyclical and the P&L in any one year is a poor guide to value. We do not use a spot multiple or a current-year P/E as the primary method, because both would capitalise a single point in the coal cycle and ignore the capex and depletion that follow.

The cost of capital build is shown below. The company reports in US dollars, so the risk-free rate is the house USD government yield, the mature-market equity risk premium and the Indonesia country risk premium are house inputs, and the beta is the industry median from the house regression set. The result is a WACC of 10.8%, with a cost of equity of 12.7%. The engine's pre-tax debt cost is the house macro corporate spread (7.0%), but IATA's own rupiah debt is more expensive: the Series B and C bonds and the Mayapada/Victoria bank facilities carry double-digit rupiah coupons [S12 Notes 18/20], and the P&L's interest line is consistent with the cost of debt in the assumptions file. We add an explicit company premium of 0.8% so the WACC reflects the actual debt stack; the WACC table shows it as its own line, not a hidden illiquidity premium. We use the market-value debt weight implied by the balance sheet and share price rather than a target mix, because the balance sheet is already levered and the DCF should reflect the financing in place.

The primary DCF is a thirty-year life model with no terminal value. The operating IUP-OPs run to 2028-2033 with extensions in process, so the model assumes the extension process succeeds; it runs thirty years, below the reserve life at the planned volume, and applies no terminal value because no renewal beyond the current applications is archived [S12 Note 1g; F5]. The present value is concentrated in the first decade [S12]. The DCF uses a sustaining capex of 1.16 per tonne, the FY2025 direct-ownership additions excluding the APE fleet build [S12 Note 10]; the fleet and the mining-property acquisitions are growth and are not deducted as maintenance. At our base assumptions the DCF produces an enterprise value of US$169.2m and an equity value of Rp76 per share after net debt and the non-operating investment bridge [S12]. The DCF is sensitive to the realised price and to capex; the sensitivity table shows the range. The model stops with 92.3 Mt of reserves still in the ground; we do not value that tail because the operating IUP-OPs run to 2028-2033 with extensions in process [S12 Note 1g] and a further renewal beyond the current applications is not archived. The port/conveyor programme is carried as capex with no quantified volume or cost benefit, because the archive discloses the spend but not the uplift [S5].

The EV/EBITDA cross-check uses the peer median, applied to the data pack's LTM EBITDA (which falls back to FY2025). The peer median is 6.4, not a blend with IATA's own five-year average: that average spans the aviation-to-coal pivot and the depressed-EBITDA years, so it is not a through-cycle multiple [S0]. The leg produces Rp38, -50.5% below the DCF, because the peer multiple is applied to a trough LTM EBITDA while the DCF prices the ramp and the normalised cash margin; the divergence is a metric problem, not a value contradiction. We weight the DCF 71% and the multiple 29% because the DCF captures the capex and depletion that the multiple ignores. The dividend-yield method carries zero weight because the company pays no dividend [S0, S12].

The valuation bridge adds the full discretionary-fund balance at 30 June 2026, US$18.8m: the Scotts and Regency funds are short-term investments managed on a discretionary basis and marked at fair value through profit or loss, and they sit outside the mining cash flows [S13 Note 13]. We use the 30 June 2026 balance because net debt is taken at the same date; the FY2025 balance was lower [S12 Note 13]. We do not add the reclamation provision because it is small at the balance-sheet date, and we do not add any value for the new controller's intentions because no transaction or plan is archived [S12, S4]. The post-balance-sheet review is in the assumptions file; the material events are the control change and rename, the pending RKAB revision, the port/conveyor programme and the H1-2026 liquidity squeeze [S4, S5, S8, S13].

The two commodity-card cross-checks are shown here. The dividend-capacity anchor is not a paid yield: the company pays 0.0% and has no dividend record [S0, S12], so the relevant capacity measure is the FY2027E FCFE yield at the current price, 2.6% before any payout [S0]. A normal payout would be a fraction of that, not the high-single-digit yield the market would need to justify the price as an income name. On EV/reserves, the DCF enterprise value of US$169.2m against 298 Mt of stated reserves [F5] is the relevant comparison; the market's IDR2,939.9bn capitalisation plus net debt is far above that on the same reserve base [S0]. The IDX coal anchor is normally dividend capacity; IATA does not pay, so the market must be using a price-recovery/volume anchor, which is the bet this report is testing.

The reverse DCF is the cleanest way to state the disagreement. At Rp94 the market is capitalising a value that requires the FY2027E newc benchmark to be about 1.2 times our deck path — roughly US$137/t — with IATA's quality discount unchanged [S0, S8, deck]. Translated at our long-run realisation, that is an ASP close to the HBA III marker, not a repeat of the high-calorie war premium; the price is therefore assuming a modestly better price, a lower capex intensity or a volume path above the plan, not an extreme outcome. We can source none of those today. The price is a bet on a better outcome than the company's own disclosed economics support, but the gap is not wide enough for a SELL.

What today's price implies is not absurd in a bull market: coal equities can re-rate, and a new controlling shareholder can change the story. But the fundamental value is Rp72, and the gap is -23.2% — enough for REDUCE, not SELL. The DCF and the multiple point the same way, although the multiple is much lower because it uses trough LTM EBITDA [S0, S12]. We would need a sourced improvement in the realised-to-benchmark spread, a contracted volume path with lower capex, a refinancing, or a corporate action that puts cash or assets into the listed entity to change that view [S8, S11, S12].

A life-of-asset DCF values the tonnes the company can economically extract, prices them at a through-cycle level and subtracts the capital needed to extract them. It is the right frame for a depleting asset because it does not assume the business lasts forever and it makes the reinvestment requirement explicit. The weakness is that the answer is sensitive to the long-run price and the discount rate, so the analysis is only as good as the sourced price anchor and the cost curve. That is why the report cross-checks the DCF against a multiple and a reverse DCF rather than presenting a single point estimate.

The downside risks are ranked by likelihood and impact. The highest-likelihood risk is the quota: the 2026 national RKAB was cut, only 2.0 Mt was approved as the initial quota and the revision to the company's request was still pending in August, and the H1 revenue decline was attributed to the quota [S6, S8, S5]. The highest-impact risk is the price: a lower low-calorie realisation would compress an already thin cash margin, and the product has no pricing power [S8]. The balance-sheet risk is the refinancing of the matured Series B bond at a higher rate or on tighter terms, with cash of US$1.2m at the H1-2026 date and factoring liabilities of US$8.1m [S13]. The inventory risk is the US$37.6m stockpile, of which coal is US$26.6m [S13 Note 8]; an NRV writedown or an unsold-tonne/quality problem would hit equity and cash. The operational risk is contractor concentration and mine-plan execution at KPP [S11]. The governance risk is the new controlling shareholder's intentions, the low free float, the unresolved special-board status and the undisclosed pledge status [S4, S14, S15]. The tax risk is the step from the FY2025 effective rate to the statutory rate [S12 Note 2n]. The macro risk is a stronger rupiah or a higher domestic interest-rate path, both of which raise the discount rate and the debt cost.

The bear case assumes the RKAB approval stalls, so volume is held near the FY2026 rate, the Series B refinancing carries a higher coupon, and the H1-2026 stockpile forces an NRV writedown that raises the cash cost; the low-calorie price fades faster than the quality discount narrows. The bull case assumes the RKAB revision lands early, KPP delivers the long-run ramp ahead of schedule, the refinancing clears at the existing coupon, and the port/conveyor programme trims the per-tonne cost. The scenarios shock the same price and volume drivers in opposite directions; the bear's deeper volume shock reflects the approved-quota cap rather than an arbitrary asymmetry [S6, F34, S13].

The bear case is valued at Rp12 and the bull case at Rp130, with probabilities of 25%, 50% and 25% respectively. The base case carries half the probability because it is the most likely path: the company has a signed contractor ramp and a large reserve base, but the quota and the price are not under its control. The bear case is not a liquidation scenario; it is the same mine plan at the FY2026 volume, a higher debt cost and an inventory writedown, which is the realistic downside for a price-taking producer with a quota cap.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A published RKAB approval at or above the requested volume would remove the quota overhang. A sustained realised price at or above the HBA III marker would narrow the quality discount. A refinancing at or below the existing coupon and a reduction in the stockpile would remove two of the bear's drivers. Conversely, a materially higher coupon, a missed coupon on the matured tranche, an NRV writedown or a related-party transaction that moves cash out of the listed entity would confirm the bear case. We monitor the monthly HBA III print, the RKAB announcement, the quarterly cash-flow statement, inventory turnover, the factoring balance and the bond trustee notices [S8, S12, S13].

The strongest honest case against our REDUCE is that the market is capitalising the new controlling shareholder's optionality, a better contract mix and a successful refinancing. A 7.0 Mt producer with a 298 Mt reserve base and a new owner could in principle re-rate, and the stock already trades at Rp94 against its one-year low of Rp54. Our answer is that optionality is not a source of fundamental value until it is contracted or funded, and the current cash flows do not support the price even on the company's own volume plan; but the gap is a REDUCE, not a SELL, because the corrected capex and the HBA III pricing leave real value in the asset. If the new owner announces a funded expansion, an offtake agreement at a better realised price, a refinancing that removes the liquidity overhang or an asset injection at a fair valuation, we will re-underwrite.

Coal equities can stay expensive for a long time when the market is pricing a change of control or a supply shock, because the narrative is not directly observable in the cash-flow statement. The discipline is to separate the value of the existing assets from the value of the option, and to require a source for the option before putting it in the base case. That is particularly important in Indonesia, where a new controlling shareholder can change the strategy quickly but where the minority shareholder has limited visibility into the plan until it is announced.

Ownership is concentrated and changing. PT Karya Pacific Investama held 60.4% as of October 2026, up from 48.8% at the end of 2025; MNC Asia Holding held 18.8% at the end of 2025 and the company states it is no longer part of the MNC group [S4, S12 Note 27]. The free float is 7.2% and the insider share is 60.6% [S0]. The FY2025 accounts still name MNC Asia Holding as the ultimate parent and Hary Tanoesoedibjo as the ultimate beneficial owner, because the control change was completed after the balance-sheet date; readers should treat the current ownership table as the authoritative one [S12 Note 1, S4]. The new controller's group structure and any pledge of the controlling stake are not disclosed in the archive, so the pledged-share risk cannot be quantified. The stock's special-board status is also unresolved: it entered the special monitoring board in 2024 [S15] and the September 2026 exit list does not include it [S14], so a full-call-auction regime and a 7.2% float remain investability constraints.

Related-party dealings are disclosed and modest in size but structurally important. At FY2025, related-party liabilities were about six per cent of total liabilities, mostly trade payables to PT Karya Pacific Shipping and other group entities, and related-party assets were under one per cent of total assets [S12 Note 26]. There were no related-party revenue transactions disclosed [S12 Note 26]. In H1-2026 the cash-flow statement shows US$8.0m of new related-party other-payables funding as cash fell [S13], which is a related-party liquidity dependence rather than a revenue transaction. The concern is forward-looking: as the controlling group changes, the potential for related-party sales, purchases or asset transfers rises, and the minority has a small float and limited ability to block them. We would treat a large related-party transaction at a non-market price as a governance red flag.

The auditor for FY2025 was KAP Kanaka Puradiredja, Suhartono, with engagement partner Yoyo Sukaryo Djenal and a fee disclosed in the annual report [S8]. The auditor's report is scanned in the archived PDF and the opinion wording could not be text-verified, so we do not assert an unqualified opinion; the accounts were filed with the IDX and the audit report is part of the filing [S12]. The company has no dividend record, so there is no dividend policy to test [S0]. The board and commissioners were changed at the June 2026 AGMS alongside the name change, which is normal after a control transfer but reduces the continuity of oversight [S6].

ESG exposures are typical for Indonesian thermal coal: land use and rehabilitation, water and dust, mine safety, and the long-run demand risk from the energy transition. The company has reclamation provisions and a sustainability report, but the provisions are small relative to the mining footprint, and the archive does not contain a detailed mine-closure cost estimate [S12, S8]. The energy-transition risk is already in the valuation through the long-run price anchor and the declining global demand path; it is not a separate ESG overlay [S8].

Indonesian coal governance is a live investment variable because the controlling family or group can direct related-party transactions, choose the auditor and set the dividend policy. The minority's protections are the listing rules, the independent commissioner and the disclosure regime, not a controlling shareholder's goodwill. A small free float magnifies the effect: a block trade or a margin call on a pledged controlling stake can move the price far more than the fundamental news. That is why the ownership table, the related-party note and the board composition are read alongside the cash-flow statement.

The near-term catalyst calendar is dominated by the balance sheet. The rupiah bond Series B reached its 6 October 2026 maturity, and the archive records neither repayment nor refinancing; the terms will tell us whether the company can fund the ramp without new equity [S12]. The H1-2026 stockpile and the US$8.1m factoring balance are the other near-term monitors: a reduction would ease the liquidity squeeze, while an NRV writedown would confirm the inventory risk [S13]. The ESDM decision on the mid-year RKAB revision is the other near-term event; approval at or above the requested volume would validate the KPP ramp, while a delay would push the volume recovery into 2027 [S8, S5]. The Q3 2026 results, expected in November, will show whether the H2 recovery management guided to is materialising [S13].

The medium-term catalysts are the first full year of the KPP contract and the port/conveyor programme. If KPP delivers the long-run run-rate in 2027 and the port works reduce the shipping bottleneck, the volume and cost lines could beat our base case [S11, S5]. A dividend initiation is not in our forecast and there is no policy to support it, but a sustained free-cash-flow improvement would make it possible; we would treat the first dividend as a signal rather than a base-case assumption [S0, S12].

The KPIs we watch between updates are: the monthly HBA III print and the ICI-5 index; the quarterly sales volume and realised ASP; the cash cost per tonne and the shipping cost per tonne; capex and the port/conveyor spend; net debt and the refinancing of the matured bond; the RKAB approval and any quota revision; and the special-board and free-float status [S8, S12, S14]. Each of these is a line in the model, so a change in any one of them flows straight into the target rather than sitting in a qualitative note.

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: ANCHORED ON THE LAST ACTUAL AND THE COMPANY PLAN, WITH THE FY2026 QUOTA OVERHANG EXPLICIT. FY2025 sales were 3.51 Mt against 3.42 Mt produced [F2/F4/S8]. The company's 2026 RKAB request is 7.85 Mt [F10/S3] and it has signed a five-year mining-services contract with PT Kalimantan Prima Persada (KPP Mining, Astra group) that lifts output from about 3 Mt in the first year toward 7 Mt a year [S11]. But the 2026 national RKAB was cut to about 600 Mt from 790 Mt actual in 2025 [S8], only 2 Mt was approved as IATA's initial 2026 quota [F34/S6], the request for 7.8-7.85 Mt was still being processed in August 2026 [S6, S5, S3], and 1H2026 revenue fell 16.5% yoy to USD33.4m [F11/S13] with management attributing the decline to the government production quota [S5]. We therefore model FY2026E at 3.2 Mt (H1 run-rate plus a partial H2 recovery if the mid-year RKAB revision lands), then FY2027E 6.5 Mt and 7.0 Mt from FY2028E as the KPP ramp and the RKAB request are delivered. Holding the 2 Mt approved quota would ignore the signed contractor ramp; jumping straight to 7.85 Mt would ignore the unapproved revision.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: CALIBRATED ON THE LAST ACTUAL, WITH THE FY2026 WAR-PREMIUM WEDGE EXPLICIT. FY2025 revenue of USD79.64m [S8] over FY2025 sales of 3.51 Mt [F2] gives a blended ASP of USD22.69/t, which is 0.209 of the FY2025A newc average of USD108.4/t and about 62% of the HBA III 2025 average of USD36.50/t [F27/S8]. The long-run ratio is that 0.209-0.21, and it reproduces the last actual at the deck's long-run newc anchor (USD105/t x 0.21 = about USD22/t). The FY2025-26 newc spike to USD137/t is a 6,000 kcal war premium that does not reach IATA's 3,400 kcal product: the company's own HBA III 2026 estimate is USD32-35/t [S8 p.86], which at its 2025 HBA III realisation implies an ASP of about USD20-21/t. We therefore set the FY2026E newc ratio at 0.152 (USD20.8/t) and step it back toward the last-actual 0.21 as the war premium fades (0.180 in FY2027E, 0.195 in FY2028E, 0.21 from FY2029E). The single departure from the last-actual ratio is the year in which the newc benchmark spikes, not the long run; the long-run value is not fitted to the spike. The engine's calibration gate is therefore manually reconciled: at the FY2025A benchmark and the last-actual 0.209 ratio the model reproduces the FY2025 actual, while the FY2026E 0.152 is the sourced HBA III-implied wedge [S8 p.86/F27/F29].

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: No DMO cap is applied because the LK does not disclose what share of IATA's tonnes is sold under the domestic-market obligation at the USD70/t cap; the domestic/export split is about half each [S12 Note 29], and a blanket cap on half the book would override the actual realised domestic ASP of Rp315,816/t that is already inside the calibrated realisation ratio [S8]. The DMO cap is kept as a scenario risk in §5 instead. Sources: S12, S8.

assumptions.label: Cost-intensity factor (bcm-per-tonne equivalent; not a physical strip ratio)
assumptions.basis: This is a pure cost-intensity factor, not a physical strip ratio. Set to 1.0 so the cost block reads the observed cash cost per tonne; no archived source discloses IATA's bcm moved or a mine-plan strip ratio (the company reports direct costs by line only [S12 Note 30]). Using an unsourced bcm ratio would add a second unknown to a cost base already printed in dollars per tonne. The per-tonne cost (cost_per_bcm) is the calibrated FY2025 actual, and the sensitivity table shocks this intensity factor as a cost multiplier.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: BACKED OUT OF THE FY2025 LK SO THE MODEL REPRODUCES THE LAST ACTUAL. FY2025 direct costs were USD35.086m, of which royalties USD5.694m [F9] and fixed-asset depreciation USD2.128m were charged in direct costs [S12 Note 30]; that leaves USD27.264m of cash cost ex-royalty ex-D&A, or USD7.77/t on 3.51 Mt of sales (F2). Note that 2024 cash cost was far higher (USD14.8/t) because of USD12.2m of subcontractor cost and a different mine mix; the 2025 print reflects APE's start-up and the contractor reorganisation, and it is the last actual, so it is the anchor. Held flat in real terms; fuel is separated out through fuel_share and escalated with Brent.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: FY2025 fuel expense of USD5.778m [S12 Note 30] over the USD27.264m cash cost ex-royalty ex-D&A gives 21.2%, so 0.21. This lets the model escalate fuel with Brent without double counting.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Carried inside cost_per_bcm (intensity 1.0) so the lines are not double counted; the mining, hauling, barging and port cost stack is expressed as one per-tonne cash cost backed out of the FY2025 LK [S12 Note 30/31].

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regime)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 royalty of USD5.694m [F9/S12 Note 30] over FY2025 revenue of USD79.637m [S8] = 7.15%. The LK does not print the HBA band, and IATA is an IUP-OP holder, so the deck's IUPK table must not be applied; the flat rate is the effective rate the LK shows being paid. Held flat; §5 tests the upside royalty risk.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: Port management fee and contractor revenue: FY2025 other revenue was USD1.418m [S12 Note 29 geography table]. Held flat in nominal terms as a small non-mining line.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Port-management services are fee-based; 30% gross margin assumed because the LK does not split the cost of the port line. Immaterial at about 2% of revenue.

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 total fixed-asset depreciation was USD2.354m [F8/S12 Note 10]; mine-property amortisation charged to production was nil in FY2025 (USD25,527 in FY2024) [S12 Note 11], so the full D&A charge is the fixed-asset line. Over 3.51 Mt [F2] that is USD0.67/t. Held flat in real terms and applied to the higher volumes; the port and conveyor capex adds to the depreciable base, so holding the per-tonne charge rather than letting it fall with volume is the neutral choice.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: SUSTAINING ONLY; THE APE FLEET BUILD IS GROWTH AND IS EXCLUDED. FY2025 acquisition of fixed assets was USD12.565m [F42/S12 cash-flow statement and Note 10]. Note 10 splits that total between USD4.076m of direct-ownership additions (buildings, machinery, vehicles [F43]) and USD8.489m of right-of-use mining-equipment additions [F44] — the start-up fleet built for the APE ramp. The fleet is growth, as the report itself says, so the sustaining base is the USD4.076m direct-ownership portion, or USD1.16/t on 3.51 Mt of sales [F2]. The old USD2.5/t averaged the fleet build into sustaining and rounded up, double counting growth; it is superseded. The separate USD12.636m of mining-property/exploration acquisition is also growth and is excluded, and the Rp200bn port/conveyor programme stays separately in capex_other. For transparency the basis discloses the alternate rates: FY2024 total additions of USD2.659m [F47] over 3.664 Mt [F1] is 0.73/t [F45/F46], and the two-year total is 2.12/t; §4 and the sensitivity show the range. Anchoring the FY2025 direct-ownership portion is the last-actual maintenance rate, not a haircut to make the DCF work.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Management flagged a Rp200bn (about USD12m at the deck's IDR/USD) programme for port and conveyor infrastructure to accelerate the recovery [S5, 10 Aug 2026 article link]. Carried as a one-off FY2026E expansion capex; no recurring expansion spend is assumed because no other project has a sourced budget in this window.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital was USD6.405m on revenue of USD79.637m, about 8.0% [S0]. The three-year average is negative because 2023 and 2024 were funded by payables, but the last actual is positive and a growing volume book will absorb inventory and receivables, so we carry 8% rather than the negative historical average. Source: S0 data pack (S0 is citable for reported financials through fin. placeholders, not for a fact entry).

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: LAST ACTUAL FOR THE EXPLICIT YEARS, STATUTORY RATE AFTER. FY2025 income tax of USD1.463m on pre-tax profit of USD9.732m was 15.0% [S12 P&L]. No tax concession or binding facility is disclosed in the LK: the statutory Indonesian corporate rate is 22% [S12 Note 2n; macro deck], the FY2024 effective rate was 36.7% and the FY2023 rate 17.3%, so the 15% print is a single-year effective rate, not a permanent regime. We keep 15% for the five explicit forecast years (FY2026E-FY2030E) as the rate the LK shows being paid, then step to the 22% statutory rate for FY2031E onward. A flat 15% for thirty years would assume an unsourced permanent benefit; the step is the most likely long-run tax rate and is tested in the bear.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The rupiah bonds carry 11.25% (Series B, due Oct 2026) and 11.50% (Series C, due Oct 2028), and the Mayapada/Victoria bank facilities carry 9-12% [S12 Notes 18/20]. A 10% blended cost of debt is consistent with that stack and with the FY2025 finance expense of USD5.048m on average debt.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income of USD0.227m on opening cash of USD3.298m is 6.9%; we carry 7% [S12 P&L and cash-flow statement].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new net borrowing assumed: gross debt is held at the FY2025 level. The bond Series B reached its 6 October 2026 maturity and no commitment is in the archive, so the neutral reading is a refinancing at maturity, not a repayment from cash flow; a higher coupon would lower value [S12].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Nil: the FY2025 other-income line was a net expense of USD0.566m and includes bank charges and tax items that are not a recurring operating driver [S12 Note 33].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025 minorities absorbed USD0.659m of USD8.269m net profit, 8.0% [S12 P&L]; the minority balances are small and volatile, so 8% is carried flat.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: ZERO BY RECORD: the company has paid no dividend in the price history (S0 dps_ttm 0; no dividends in the data pack) and the FY2025 LK shows no distribution; cash has gone to mining-property acquisition and the port programme. The dividend-capacity anchor therefore does not apply to the paid stream; §4 discusses the capacity rather than a current yield.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No new shares assumed: the February-2025 rights issue took the count to 31,275.8m shares [S12 Note 27], and no further corporate action is disclosed.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for USD reporting; the coal deck's long-run newc anchor is held flat in real terms [S8], so 2% is the neutral nominal allowance rather than a volume-growth assumption.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 selling expenses of USD23.206m plus operating expenses of USD5.435m, less the depreciation inside them (USD0.143m + USD0.078m), give USD28.420m of cash opex on USD79.637m of revenue = 35.7% [S12 P&L and Note 31/32]. That is the last actual rate and replaces the engine's 32.6% three-year average, which is flattered by the higher 2023-24 revenue base. Selling costs are dominated by coal shipping (USD22.5m), which should scale with volume, so a constant percentage of revenue is a reasonable neutral treatment.

challenges.challenge: capex_unit of USD2.5/t double-counts the APE start-up fleet as sustaining capex. The basis says FY2025 fixed-asset acquisitions of USD12.565m 'include the APE fleet build' (growth), yet averages it with FY2024's USD2.659m (0.73/t) and then rounds UP to 2.5. At 6.5-7.0 Mt that is USD16.3-17.5m/yr versus ~USD5.1m at the FY2024 sustaining rate, while FY2027E FCFF is only USD12.0m. If the fleet build is excluded as the report itself says it is growth, the DCF roughly doubles and the SELL no longer holds.
challenges.answer: FATAL accepted. Note 10 splits the FY2025 USD12.565m fixed-asset additions into USD4.076m of direct-ownership additions and USD8.489m of right-of-use mining equipment, the APE start-up fleet. We treat the fleet as growth and set capex_unit to the direct-ownership portion, USD1.16/t, instead of the old USD2.5/t that averaged the fleet build into sustaining and rounded up. The basis discloses the FY2024 0.73/t and two-year 2.12/t alternatives, and the model is re-run: the DCF rises from about Rp39 to about Rp76 and the rating moves from SELL to REDUCE, target Rp72, exactly the direction the challenge predicted. The USD12.6m mining-property acquisitions and the Rp200bn port/conveyor programme remain growth and are excluded from sustaining capex.

challenges.challenge: The bridge adds only USD11.397m of 'other investments' [F13], but S12 Note 13's two discretionary funds sum to USD20.015m at 31 Dec 2025 (11.397 Scotts + 8.618 Regency) and USD18.811m at 30 Jun 2026 (10.712 + 8.099). The valuation uses 30 Jun 2026 net debt of USD56.5m, so it should carry the 30 Jun 2026 balance; the omission is USD7.4-8.6m, or about Rp4.4-5.1/share.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The bridge now carries the full Note 13 balance at 30 June 2026, USD18.811m: Scotts USD10.712m plus Regency USD8.099m, both short-term discretionary funds at fair value through profit or loss [F35/S13 Note 13]. The old bridge used only the Scotts FY2025 balance, a date mismatch as well as an omission. We use the 30 June 2026 balance because net debt is taken at the same date. The equity value rises by about USD7.4m, or roughly Rp4.3/share.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA leg applies 7.44x, the average of the 2.81x peer median (from the COAL comps) and IATA's own five-year average of ~12.1x (2 x 7.44 - 2.81). At the peer median the leg's equity value is near zero because peer-multiple EV roughly equals net debt. The report's explanation that 'peers trade at a premium for their own growth and dividend profiles' is reversed: the applied multiple is ~2.6x the peer median. The own five-year average spans the 2022 aviation-to-coal pivot and depressed-EBITDA years.
challenges.answer: Accepted on method: the company now uses the peer median, not the peer/own-history blend. We cannot reproduce the 2.81x number from the engine's COAL peer set: the median of the 14 COAL data packs is 6.44x [S0], and IATA's own five-year average is 8.44x, not 12.1x. Even so, the own average spans the aviation-to-coal pivot, so it is not a through-cycle multiple and is no longer used. At 6.44x the EV/EBITDA leg is Rp38, about 50% below the Rp76 DCF, because the peer multiple is applied to a trough LTM EBITDA of USD15.9m while the DCF prices the ramp and the normalised margin; §4 states that divergence and keeps the DCF at 71% weight.

challenges.challenge: The price driver is Newcastle 6,000 kcal at a 0.21 ratio, although the method card says coal realisation keys off HBA/ICI and IATA's product is 3,400 kcal GAR. The company's own HBA III 2026 estimate is USD32-35/t [S8 p.86]; at its 2025 realisation of ~61-62% of HBA III that implies an ASP of ~USD19-21/t, not the model's FY2026E USD28.77/t (0.21 x newc 137.0). The report argues the Newcastle war premium does not reach the product, yet the model capitalises it. FY2026E revenue of USD93.5m also needs H2 of USD60.1m, +80% HoH from H1's USD33.4m.
challenges.answer: Accepted. FY2026E is now priced on the company's own HBA III 2026 estimate of USD32-35/t [F47/F48/S8 p.86] at its 2025 HBA III realisation of about 62%: the FY2026E newc ratio is 0.152, giving an ASP of about USD20.8/t instead of USD28.8/t. From FY2027E the newc ratio returns to the last-actual 0.21 as the war premium fades. The resulting FY2026E revenue is about USD68m, which reconciles to H1 revenue of USD33.4m plus a modest H2 recovery at 3.2 Mt; the old USD93.5m required H2 to rise 80% HoH. The EBITDA impact is about USD14m in FY2026E, but the DCF effect is small because FY2026E is a half-year stub; the long-run realisation is unchanged at the FY2025 actual. Newc remains the forecastable scaling index only because the deck's HBA III series has no forecast path.

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative says volume 'stays near the FY2026 rate' (~3.2 Mt), but the bear shock is a.volume x0.95 (6.18 Mt). At 3.2 Mt the equity would be near zero, not Rp14. The bear also omits two concrete balance-sheet risks the report names: refinancing the matured Series B bond at a higher coupon and the new H1-2026 factoring of USD8.1m.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The bear volume shock is now 0.5x, which holds FY2027E at about 3.2 Mt, exactly the narrative's quota-held case; the old 0.95x contradicted it. The bear also adds a cost-of-debt shock of +2pp for the Series B refinancing and a cost_per_bcm shock of +1.0/t for the H1-2026 stockpile/NRV problem. The bull mirrors both cost and debt shocks in the opposite direction, and the volume asymmetry is justified in qc_justifications by the approved-quota cap [F34/S6], not by analyst caution. The probability-weighted target falls to Rp72 and the bear case to Rp12.

challenges.challenge: H1-2026 inventory is USD37.6m (70% of current assets; ~47% of FY2025 revenue) and rose from USD34.8m at Dec-2025; cash fell to USD1.2m, factoring rose to USD8.1m from nil, and current liabilities (USD69.7m) exceed current assets (USD54.0m) [S13]. The report dismisses inventory as 'normal for a coal producer' without turnover or NRV analysis. A stockpile writedown or an unsold-tonne/quality problem would hit equity.
challenges.answer: Accepted. §3 now analyses the inventory: USD37.6m at H1-2026, of which coal is USD26.6m, against H1 direct costs of USD21.3m, so the stockpile covers more than a year of cost of sales; that is not a normal working stock and an NRV writedown is a live risk. The current assets/liabilities, cash and factoring numbers are all in the report and the facts file. The bear case carries the NRV problem through the cost_per_bcm shock. The H1-2026 figures are sourced to the filing, not the old FY2025 balance sheet.

challenges.challenge: The report applies a 0.0% liquidity discount despite a 7.2% free float, an unconfirmed exit from the special monitoring board (full call auction), and no disclosure of controlling-stake pledges. The 0% discount follows an ADTV input of IDR106.6bn/day, which is implausible for a 7.2%-float name and is not disclosed or tested.
challenges.answer: Accepted on disclosure and risk; the model's 0% line is unchanged because the house rule keys the liquidity discount on the data pack's three-month ADTV, which is IDR106.6bn/day [S0], far above the house thresholds, not on the free float. That input is now disclosed in the report and the mkt.adtv placeholder, and §5/§6 carry the 7.2% float, the unresolved special-board exit and the undisclosed controlling-stake pledge as explicit investability risks. We did not apply an ad-hoc float discount on top of the house rule; the risk is carried in the bear narrative and the signposts instead.

challenges.challenge: The method card requires a dividend-capacity cross-check and EV/reserves, and §3 says '§4 discusses capacity', but §4 contains no dividend-capacity yield, payout capacity, EV/reserves or cost-curve quartile. At FY2027E NP of USD22.7m and normalising capex, a 40-50% payout would be a 5-7% yield at Rp94 — the IDX coal anchor the market may be using.
challenges.answer: Accepted. §4 now carries both cross-checks the commodity card requires. The dividend-capacity anchor is the FY2027E FCFE yield at the current price, disclosed from the model, because the company pays no dividend; the report states that a normal payout would be a fraction of that and that IATA cannot be an income anchor. On EV/reserves, the DCF enterprise value is set against the stated reserve base and compared with the market capitalisation plus net debt. The report states that the IDX coal market normally uses dividend capacity, that IATA does not pay, and that the market must therefore be using a price-recovery/volume anchor, which is the bet the report tests.

challenges.challenge: The DCF stops at FY2055E with no terminal value, leaving ~88 Mt of stated reserves (298 Mt less ~210 Mt mined) and 1,427 Mt of resources unvalued; the USD12m port/conveyor capex is expensed in FY2026 with none of its cost or volume benefit modelled.
challenges.answer: Accepted. §4 now quantifies the unvalued tail: the DCF stops with the remaining reserve line still in the ground and does not value it because the operating IUP-OPs run to 2028-2033 with extensions in process [S12 Note 1g], so the licence-extension path, not the reserve life, is the binding cut-off. The port/conveyor programme is carried as capex with no volume or cost benefit modelled, because the archive discloses the spend but not the uplift [S5]; we explicitly rule out a benefit rather than capitalise one. The resource base beyond reserves is a free option, not base NAV.

challenges.challenge: Tax is held at 15.0% for 30 years. The FY2024 effective rate was 36.7%, the statutory rate used in the WACC is 22%, and the COAL peers cluster at 21-26%. A flat 15% assumes the FY2025 benefit persists; a step-up to 22% cuts FCFF by about USD2m/yr and the target by roughly Rp5-8.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The tax rate is 15% for FY2026E-FY2030E, the rate the LK shows being paid, then steps to the statutory 22% [S12 Note 2n] from FY2031E. No concession is disclosed, and the FY2024 effective rate was 36.7%, so a permanent 15% was unsupported. The step cuts FY2031E and later FCFF and the target by roughly the Rp5-8 the challenge estimated. §3 states the step and §5 carries the tax risk.

challenges.challenge: strip_ratio is set to 1.0, the lowest in the COAL comps (peers 2.85-10.0), with no source; the report labels it 'bcm per tonne or cost-intensity factor'. A reader or comps screen will see a 1:1 strip ratio, and no source discloses IATA's bcm. The value is unaffected only because cost_per_bcm is a per-tonne actual.
challenges.answer: Accepted. strip_ratio is relabelled a pure cost-intensity factor, not a physical bcm-per-tonne ratio, and the basis states that the per-tonne cost is the calibrated FY2025 actual. No archived source discloses IATA's bcm moved or a mine-plan strip ratio [S12 Note 30]. The value is unchanged; only the label and the basis are corrected.

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF solves the price for newc and concludes the price is a 'war premium' (1.2x = USD146). At the implied ASP (0.21 x 146 = USD30.7/t), IATA would realise ~67% of the current HBA III spot of USD45.53/t, only modestly above its 2025 61-62% ratio — not a war premium. The conclusion is an artefact of the newc proxy.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The report no longer calls the price a war premium. The reverse DCF shows a newc factor of about {{rev.factor}} (roughly {{rev.implied_value}}), and at the long-run realisation the implied ASP is close to the HBA III marker, not a repeat of the high-calorie spike. The engine's reverse DCF is on newc because the deck's HBA III series has no forecast path; §4 translates the implied newc to the HBA III realisation and states that the price is a modest premium, not a war premium. The lower FY2026E newc realisation also removes the capitalised spike.

challenges.challenge: The WACC uses a pre-tax debt cost of 6.99% (rf 4.99% + macro corporate spread 2.00%), not the 10-11.5% rupiah bond/bank cost described in S12 or the assumptions file's cost_of_debt of 10%. The report claims the debt cost comes from S12. A 10% kd adds ~60bp to WACC and trims the DCF ~5%.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The WACC now carries an explicit company premium of 0.83pp on the COE so the resulting WACC matches the 10% pre-tax debt cost, adding about 61bp to the WACC and trimming the DCF by about 5%; the WACC table shows the premium as its own line, and the P&L interest line already uses the 10% cost of debt [S12 Notes 18/20]. This is a disclosed debt-cost adjustment, not a hidden illiquidity premium. §4 explains the engine's macro spread and the company-specific stack.

flags.message: FY+1 priced at FY2025A benchmark and volume gives EBITDA 5.7 vs the actual 18.0 (-68%): reconcile costs, royalty or realisation with the filing, or justify the change
flags.justification: The engine re-prices FY+1 at the FY2025A newc benchmark with the FY2026E newc ratio, but IATA's 3,400 kcal product is priced off HBA III, not newc. The stable calibration is the HBA III ratio: FY2025 ASP of USD22.69m/3.51 Mt over the HBA III 2025 average of USD36.50/t is 62.2% [F27/S8], and the FY2026E ASP of USD20.8/t over the company's HBA III 2026 midpoint of USD33.5/t is 62.1% [S8 p.86]. The newc ratio moves only because the 6,000 kcal war premium moves (FY2025A newc 108.4 vs FY2026E 137.0), so the FY2026E 0.152 newc ratio is the same 62% HBA III realisation expressed against the spiked newc series. The FY2025 actual is reproduced at the last-actual 0.209 newc ratio; the gap is a benchmark artefact, not a cost or royalty error. [F27, F29, S8]

flags.message: a.volume moves +119% from FY2026E to FY2055E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The +119% from FY2026E 3.2 Mt to the 7.0 Mt long-run rate is the company's own ramp, not an unsourced drift: the five-year KPP Mining contract signed in Dec 2025 lifts output from about 3 Mt in the first year toward 7 Mt a year [S11], the 2026 RKAB request is 7.85 Mt [F10/S3] and the annual report targets 7.8 Mt [S8]. FY2026 is held at 3.2 Mt because only 2 Mt was approved as the initial 2026 quota [F34/S6], the revision was still pending in August [S5], and management attributes the 1H2026 revenue decline to the quota [S5].

flags.message: a.realisation moves +38% from FY2026E to FY2055E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The newc realisation rises from 0.152 in FY2026E to 0.21 long-run because the FY2026E newc benchmark is a 6,000 kcal war-premium spike (137.0) while IATA's 3,400 kcal product realisation is stable at about 62% of HBA III [F27/S8]. The long-run 0.21 is the FY2025 actual (ASP 22.69 / newc 108.4), not a drift away from it; the only departure is the war-premium year, and the long-run value is deliberately not fitted to that spike. [F2, F27, F29, S8]

flags.message: a.volume: bear 0.5 vs bull 1.05 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The downside volume shock is the approved-quota case, not a symmetric market shock: only 2.0 Mt was approved as IATA's initial 2026 quota [F34/S6] against the 6.5 Mt FY2027E base, and management attributes the H1-2026 revenue decline to the quota [S5]. A 0.5x shock holds volume near the FY2026 rate (3.2 Mt), which is the documented regulatory downside; the bull's 1.05x is the KPP contractor ramp [S11]. The asymmetry is the regulation, not analyst caution.

flags.message: a flat royalty overrides the licence schedule: justify it with the LK's effective rate
flags.justification: A flat 7.15% is the effective royalty rate the LK shows being paid: FY2025 royalty of USD5.694m [F9/S12 Note 30] over FY2025 revenue of USD79.637m [S8]. IATA is an IUP-OP holder, not IUPK [S12 Note 1g], and the LK discloses no calorific band that would let us apply the deck's IUP low/mid/high-calorie table; applying the IUPK schedule instead would be the wrong regime.

flags.message: the DCF stops after 30 years while reserves last ~93 years at FY+1 volume: extend the horizon or justify the cut
flags.justification: The 30-year cut is a value life, not a reserve life: at the 7 Mt plan the 298 Mt reserve base [F5] lasts about 42 years, but the operating IUP-OPs run only to 2028-2033 with extensions in process [S12 Note 1g]. The DCF therefore assumes the extension process succeeds for the 30-year window, stops below the full reserve life, and applies no terminal value; extending to the 93-year reserve-life arithmetic at FY2026E volume would assume successive renewals and prices that are not archived. The value of the unvalued tail is disclosed in §4 with the FY2055E remaining reserve line [F5].
